messages.subject: out of sample predictions
parts:
Hello,

I'm doing some out-of-sample predictions,
but the posterior summaries of the parameters of interest (the main parameters in the model),
when I consider the calculation of the predicted values inside nimble,
are changing as well.
In WinBUGS we add the option of using the "cut()" function. I'm aware that this is not possible in nimble.
What is the best approach of doing this?

thanks in advance
Rui

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: out of sample predictions
parts:
Hi Rui,

We don't provide a cut() function. In part this is because it's unclear what the posterior is when one uses such functionality (please see Plummer, M. (2015). Cuts in Bayesian graphical models. Statistics and Computing, 25(1), 37-43.)

In general the posterior when running the model with the predicted values (i.e., predictive nodes) and without them should be equivalent, statistically but because you also sample the predictive nodes in the latter case (which shifts which random numbers are being used to sample the parameters), the exact numerical values in the two cases won't be the same. If you're seeing that the posteriors are not equivalent then something is wrong and we could discuss further.

So I think you have two options:

a) Include the predictive nodes in the model and sample as part of the primary MCMC. The downside to this is that the MCMC spends time sampling the predictive nodes, which if you are going to thin your samples anyway (e.g., to save storage space), means you spend time getting samples you won't use. Also, this could affect mixing of the parameters because the parameter updates are done conditional on the values simulated into the predictive nodes. But doing it this way is simplest to manage.

b) Don't include the predictive nodes in the model (or include them but remove the MCMC samplers assigned to them). After you've run the MCMC, you can loop through the iterations, put the parameter values back into the model, and simulate predictive nodes given the parameter values from each of the iterations (or a thinned set of the iterations). To do this, a computationally efficient approach would be to create an expanded model with the additional predictive nodes and write a nimbleFunction that will put parameter values into that expanded model, simulate into the predictive nodes, and store the resulting predictions. A perhaps easier approach to code up quickly is just to do this directly in R via a loop, though for large models this could be slow.  Also note that unless you override it, NIMBLE won't allow simulation into nodes flagged as 'data' nodes, so it's best not to set the predictive nodes to be flagged as 'data'.

We also have cross validation capability in NIMBLE, which might be useful depending on exactly what you are trying to do. Please see help(runCrossValidate).

-Chris
